materials.label: Known-human benchmark passage
materials.content: The first map I trusted was drawn on the back of a gas bill. My father marked the bus stop with a square, the clinic with a cross, and the alley that flooded with three impatient waves. None of it was to scale. The walk looked short until I tried it carrying my brother, who had fallen asleep before we reached the bakery. Years later, studying urban planning, I met cleaner maps. They could calculate a twelve-minute journey and shade a flood zone blue. They could not show the grocer who kept a chair behind his counter for my father, or the wall we touched at night because its bricks held the day's heat. Nor did my father's map explain everything. He left out the shortcut behind the garage after an argument with its owner, and his cross for the clinic covered half a street. Memory has its own scale errors. This is not an argument against measurement. It is an argument for asking what a measure leaves out. A transport model can reveal where a route fails thousands of people; a hand-drawn map can reveal why one family takes it anyway. One view aggregates experience, while the other catches on a particular doorway. Neither deserves the last word. Useful planning needs both views, and it needs the humility to notice when neither is complete.

materials.label: Synthetic translated passage
materials.content: When the neighbourhood says mañana, it does not always mean tomorrow. Sometimes it means after the heat, when the metal chairs stop burning the backs of our legs. My aunt translates it as later, but later is too empty. Mañana carries the person who said it and the work still waiting on the table. I noticed this when I translated our community notice into English. The Spanish version asked neighbours to traer algo para compartir, to bring something for sharing. My first English sentence said, bring an item to share. It was correct, and it sounded like a rule at the airport. I changed item to plate, though not everybody brings food on a plate. One family brings ice. Another brings a speaker that works only if the cable bends near the plug. Translation makes these small problems. You gain a clear noun and you lose the room around it. At school, I was told to avoid repeating the same word, but my grandmother repeats venga, venga when she wants us to come close. The second word is not redundant. It adds the hand movement. For this reason, I no longer ask whether a translation is perfect. I ask what it lets the new reader notice, and what becomes quieter when the sentence crosses over. Sometimes I keep the Spanish word and explain it. Sometimes explanation makes the moment heavy. There is no formula. You listen, choose, and accept that a little meaning stays behind.
